headline: Szmyt drills a 56-yarder with 10 seconds left to bury the comeback
keyStat: Andre Szmyt: game-winning 56-yard FG with 0:10 left
recap:
Aaron Rodgers did everything the Steelers paid him to do. Down 21-10 at halftime in Cleveland, he engineered 14 fourth-quarter points — a 3-yard touchdown to Pat Freiermuth, then his own two-point conversion plunge — to tie the game at 24 with 1:42 left. The comeback was complete. The legend had delivered. All that remained was the kickoff.

Ninety-two seconds later, Andre Szmyt drilled a 56-yarder to win it 27-24, and Rodgers' masterpiece became a footnote. That's the cruelty of a perfect comeback: it only counts if the other team doesn't get the ball back. The Steelers left 102 seconds on the clock, and the Browns used 92 of them — plus a kicker with ice in his veins and 56 yards of leg.

Cleveland's defense built the lead with a 21-point second quarter, Pittsburgh's quarterback nearly stole it with a fourth quarter for the ages, and the whole thing was decided by a specialist. Somewhere there's a lesson about situational football. The Steelers just paid full tuition to learn it.

headline: Colts spot Washington six, then win going away 30-13
keyStat: IND outscored WSH 30-7 after falling behind 6-0
recap:
Washington opened with two field goals, took a 6-0 lead, and apparently decided that was enough offense for one Sunday. The Commanders treated the end zone like a museum exhibit for most of the afternoon — look, don't touch — before a third-quarter touchdown made the scoreboard slightly less embarrassing.

Indianapolis, meanwhile, scored 10 points in each of the final three quarters, because that's what professional offenses do. Jonathan Taylor punched in two 5-yard touchdowns, Spencer Shrader was automatic from 48, 52, and 44, and Daniel Jones ran one in himself in the fourth quarter — which is how you know it was over. When Daniel Jones is scoring rushing touchdowns, the defense has officially stopped filing paperwork.

The final indignity: Washington's 6-0 lead lasted about as long as a New Year's resolution. The Colts turned it into a 30-13 laugher without ever seeming particularly stressed, which is the most damning thing you can say about a loss. The Commanders didn't lose a football game so much as they attended one.

headline: Jameis deals three TDs, and a 98-yard pick-six at 0:00 pads the final
keyStat: Deonte Banks: 98-yard pick-six on the final play
recap:
For exactly one quarter, Arizona was the better team — 14-3, confident, rolling. Then Jameis Winston threw three touchdown passes, and the Giants spent the rest of the afternoon demonstrating why 'for exactly one quarter' was doing so much work in that sentence.

New York carried a 27-24 lead into the fourth and never gave it back. Dominic Zvada's 52-yarder with 2:11 left stretched it to two scores, and then — because this game had a sense of theater — Deonte Banks picked off a pass on the final play and housed it 98 yards as time expired. The most exciting play of the afternoon happened after the game was already over, which feels cosmically appropriate.

The 98-yarder turned a solid win into a 36-24 laugher and gave the final score a confidence it hadn't quite earned. Arizona's fourth quarter: zero points, one catastrophic donation. The rare touchdown that mattered to absolutely no one — except the final score, Deonte Banks' family, and everyone who had the Giants minus the points.

headline: Lamb’s 12-yard TD with 40 seconds left caps a 796-yard shootout
keyStat: Dak to CeeDee Lamb: game-winning 12-yd TD with 0:40 left
recap:
Houston led 16-6 at halftime and had every reason to feel good about itself. Then Dallas hung 14 points on the third quarter, and the Texans spent the rest of the afternoon discovering that a 10-point halftime lead is more of a suggestion than a plan.

This was a 796-yard shootout with zero turnovers — both offenses operating at peak efficiency, both defenses essentially cosplaying as traffic cones. Javonte Williams ran for three Dallas touchdowns. Woody Marks answered for Houston, his go-ahead score with 2:23 left putting the Texans up 30-27 and feeling, for exactly 103 seconds, like winners.

Then Dak Prescott found CeeDee Lamb for 12 yards and the win with 40 seconds on the clock, and Houston learned the oldest lesson in football: the only lead that matters is the one at 0:00. The rare shootout where both defenses can show their faces in public — because when nobody punts and nobody turns it over, what exactly were they supposed to do?

headline: Packers survive 15 scoreless minutes after Bucs pull within three
keyStat: No points scored in the final 14:49
recap:
Trey Smack's 58-yard field goal at the halftime gun looked like a footnote. It turned out to be the entire story — the three points that separated these teams at the end, doing more work than any other kick on a Sunday that belonged to kickers.

Green Bay went up 17-7 in the third quarter. Tampa Bay answered 11 seconds into the fourth. And then both offenses spent the final 14:49 producing absolutely nothing — no points, no drama, just vibes and punts. The Packers won a game in which they didn't score for the entire fourth quarter, which is either championship grit or a quiet cry for help, and the answer depends entirely on your rooting interest.

Tampa Bay got within three points with nearly a full quarter to play and never got closer. That's not a comeback falling short — that's knocking on the door for fifteen minutes without ever trying the handle. Surviving is surviving. But the Packers made it weird, and weird wins count exactly the same.

headline: Bengals outgain Jags by 114 yards, lose by five anyway
recap:
Joe Burrow threw for 414 yards. The Bengals lost by five. Somewhere in the analytics department, a spreadsheet just quietly filed for divorce.

Cincinnati outgained Jacksonville by 114 yards and turned it into 17 points, because two turnovers will do that to a stat line. Burrow was brilliant between the 20s and a rumor inside them. Cam Little, meanwhile, was perfect from everywhere that mattered — 55, 28, 54 — and the Jaguars' entire offensive philosophy appeared to be 'kick it when in doubt, which was often.'

This is the week's purest example of the oldest truth in football: yardage is a suggestion, points are the law. The Bengals did everything except the thing that counts. And the kickers — as we'll keep seeing all week — remain undefeated.

headline: Rams outgain Eagles by 243 yards, still need a 4th-quarter miracle
keyStat: Kyren Williams: 2 go-ahead TDs in the final 4:00
recap:
Philadelphia turned 172 total yards — 68 through the air, a number that should require a permit — into a 20-10 halftime lead. That's either elite efficiency or a magic trick, and for two quarters the Eagles had the Rams checking their wallets.

Then the bill came due. Kyren Williams plunged in from the 1-yard line and again from the 7 with 70 seconds left, completing a fourth-quarter comeback for a team that outgained Philadelphia by 243 yards. Let that sit: the Rams dominated every spreadsheet column for three quarters and still needed a last-minute touchdown to beat a team that barely threw the ball.

Outgaining someone by 243 yards and winning by four is the football equivalent of needing a stepstool to reach the top shelf you already own. The Eagles will take the moral victory of making a yardage massacre interesting. The Rams will take the actual victory — and a long, hard look at how 243 extra yards bought them exactly four points.

headline: Maye answers Allen’s go-ahead TD with 1:50 left, converts the 2-pointer
keyStat: NE scored the go-ahead TD + 2-pt conversion with 1:50 left
recap:
Josh Allen found Keon Coleman for 34 yards and a 26-21 lead with 4:27 left, and the missed two-pointer hung over everything like a group-chat typing indicator. You know the feeling — the message that never arrives, the dots that just keep pulsing.

Drake Maye needed 157 seconds to answer: a 23-yard strike to Efton Chism III, then a two-point conversion to Rhamondre Stevenson, and suddenly it's 29-26 Patriots with 110 seconds left. Buffalo had the lead, the crowd, and a quarterback who does this for a living. New England had a plan — and the last word.

The Bills will spend the week thinking about one missed conversion, the two points that would have changed all of Maye's fourth-quarter math. The Patriots will spend it knowing their quarterback walked into Buffalo, took the final minutes personally, and converted when it mattered. That's the difference between a typing indicator and a sent message.

headline: Bears outgain Jets 492-157; the 11-point margin is doing charity work
recap:
Chicago never trailed, led by 17, and outgained the Jets 492-157 — a 335-yard gap that should come with a wellness check. The Bears scored in all four quarters, never let it get interesting, and generally conducted themselves like a team that had somewhere better to be.

New York's lone touchdown was a 58-yard heave from Geno Smith after the score was already 23-6 — the football equivalent of tipping the valet after the car already left. It was the Jets' longest play of the day and their most meaningless, which is one way to summarize the afternoon.

The final says 11 points. The box score says it wasn't that kind of game. Somewhere the Jets' offense is still looking for those 335 yards — somebody check the lost and found.

headline: Ravens led 24-7 at half; the six-point final is a clerical error
keyStat: BAL led 24-7 at halftime; TEN’s only second-half TD came with 1:12 left
recap:
Baltimore was up 24-7 at halftime, and Tyler Loop's 64-yard field goal at the gun was the exclamation point on a paragraph that was already finished. The Ravens then spent the entire second half scoring zero points — either concerning, or the luxury of a team that knew the game ended in the second quarter.

Tennessee's first touchdown since the opening quarter came with 72 seconds left, and the two-pointer made it 24-18, and suddenly the final score was doing some very generous rounding. Respect the fight — 11 second-half points takes effort. But the scoreboard is being charitable here, and we all know it.

The Ravens won this game before halftime and spent the second half in cruise control. The Titans lost it before halftime and spent the fourth quarter making it look respectable. Both teams got what they wanted. Only one of them got what counts.

headline: All 15 Vikings points came from one right foot
keyStat: Will Reichard: 5 FGs — all 15 Vikings points
recap:
Minnesota never found the end zone and never needed to. Will Reichard kicked five field goals — from 47, 50, 33, 41, and 29 — and personally outscored the Dolphins 15-10. Read that again: the Vikings' kicker outscored an entire NFL offense.

Miami managed 77 net passing yards, which suggests the forward pass was more of a rumor in Minneapolis on Sunday. All 10 Dolphins points came in the third quarter, a brief interruption before the offense returned to its regularly scheduled programming.

This is the platonic ideal of an ugly win — five scoring drives, zero touchdowns, a final score that looks like a baseball game. When your kicker is your entire offense and you still win, that's not a game plan. That's a lifestyle. And honestly? Five-for-five will play, every single week.

headline: Broncos pull within three; Kittle answers with a 56-yard dagger
keyStat: Kittle’s 56-yd TD came 2 minutes after DEN pulled within 3
recap:
For about four minutes, the upset was alive. Denver had clawed back to 17-14, the Broncos' sideline was celebrating, and somewhere a parlay was breathing again.

Then Brock Purdy hit George Kittle for 56 yards, the lead was 10 before the celebration ended, and that was that. Two minutes — that's how long Denver's miracle lasted. The Broncos spent three quarters climbing the mountain and about 120 seconds enjoying the view.

San Francisco didn't dominate this game; it just answered every question on the test. The 49ers never trailed in the second half and treated Denver's best punch like a mosquito — annoying for a moment, irrelevant by the next drive. The Broncos get the moral victory of making it interesting. The 49ers get the actual victory, which counts for more in the standings and, one suspects, in the locker room.

headline: Chiefs score twice in 19 seconds; Raiders’ rally dies at 30-27
keyStat: KC scored 2 TDs 19 seconds apart in the 4th quarter
recap:
Las Vegas did everything right. The Raiders led in the fourth quarter, outgained Kansas City 437-399, and had the full recipe for the upset of the week.

Then Kenneth Walker III scored two rushing touchdowns 19 seconds apart, and the recipe caught fire. Nineteen seconds. That's not a collapse, that's a magic trick — now you see a lead, now you don't. To their credit, the Raiders answered with a touchdown and a two-pointer to get within three with 1:46 left, which made the ending dramatic instead of embarrassing.

But 106 seconds wasn't enough to undo 19 seconds of chaos, and that's the thing about playing Kansas City: you don't have to be worse than them. You just have to be worse than them for nineteen seconds. The Raiders were better for 59 minutes and 41 seconds. It wasn't enough. It's never enough.

headline: Seattle led big; the Chargers’ fourth quarter was a costume
keyStat: SEA led 20-3 at half; LAC committed 4 turnovers
recap:
Seattle was up 20-3 at halftime and spent the third quarter turning a comfortable lead into a commanding one. Then Justin Herbert happened — a 2-yard touchdown and a field goal in the fourth that cut it to 30-23 and gave the final score a respectability it hadn't earned.

Four Chargers turnovers say this was never a seven-point game. The final score is wearing a costume; the first three quarters are the face underneath. Seattle scored 30 points without scoring in the fourth quarter, which tells you everything about when this game was actually decided.

The Chargers' fourth quarter was spirited, commendable, and completely beside the point — a strong finish in a race that ended an hour ago. Garbage-time touchdowns count the same in the box score. They just don't count the same anywhere else.

headline: Panthers hold off 406 Goff yards behind Young’s two TDs to McMillan
keyStat: DET: 452 yards, 406 passing — and 4 field goals
recap:
Jared Goff threw for 406 yards. Detroit gained 452. The Lions lost by six, because their red zone plan was apparently 'Jake Bates from distance' — four field goals, and not much else to show for nearly half a thousand yards.

Bryce Young threw two touchdowns to Tetairoa McMillan, Chuba Hubbard ran for two more, and Carolina's 32-19 fourth-quarter lead survived a late Lions touchdown the way a good fence survives weather. The Panthers didn't need 400 yards. They needed the end zone, and they found it four times.

The math is the joke: 452 yards, 26 points — 17.4 yards per point, a ratio that should be studied by scientists. Detroit moved the ball like a contender and finished drives like a team that had somewhere else to be. Somewhere, an analytics department is screaming into a pillow.

headline: Falcons run for five TDs; Saints’ last score came down 28
keyStat: ATL rushed for 205 yards and 5 TDs
recap:
Bijan Robinson needed 86 seconds to go 59 yards and end the competitive portion of the afternoon. The opening touchdown was less a drive and more of an announcement: this is how today is going to go.

Atlanta rushed for 205 yards and five touchdowns, never turned the ball over, and led 45-17 before New Orleans scored with 73 seconds left — a touchdown thrown by backup Tyler Shough, which tells you everything about when the Saints stopped trying to win and started trying to look better. Mission partially accomplished: 24 looks much better than 17, right up until you remember the other team hung 45.

The Falcons didn't just win; they imposed their will so thoroughly that the fourth quarter was a scrimmage. New Orleans got run over all afternoon by an offense that never had to be creative. When you rush for five touchdowns and don't turn it over, you don't need creativity. You need a victory formation — which Atlanta got to practice early.
